clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in TRIM32, which encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase; the recurrent p.Asp487Asn founder variant is characteristic of the North American Hutterite population.
Typically presents as a mild, slowly progressive proximal limb-girdle weakness with onset in adulthood.
Allelic with sarcotubular myopathy (same gene, overlapping histology) and, through distinct variants, with Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 11.
Creatine kinase is usually mildly to moderately elevated.
Muscle biopsy may show dystrophic change with rimmed vacuoles or tubular aggregates.
Facial and respiratory involvement are generally mild or absent.
Cardiac involvement is uncommon, in contrast to several other limb-girdle subtypes.
Consider the diagnosis in mild adult-onset limb-girdle weakness, particularly with relevant ancestry.
reference.pathophysiology: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R8 results from biallelic variants in TRIM32 on chromosome 9q33.1, which encodes tripartite motif-containing protein 32, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags sarcomeric and cytoskeletal substrates (including actin- and desmin-associated proteins) for regulated proteasomal turnover. The recurrent p.Asp487Asn founder variant was first identified in the Hutterite population, and most disease-causing changes lie within the C-terminal NHL beta-propeller domain that mediates substrate recognition. Loss of ligase activity is thought to disturb the balance of muscle protein synthesis and degradation, impairing myofibrillar maintenance and producing slowly progressive dystrophic change, sometimes with a sarcotubular myopathy pattern that is an allelic condition. Notably, different variants in the same gene cause Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 11, illustrating that the muscular dystrophy and the ciliopathy phenotypes arise from distinct functional consequences at the TRIM32 locus.
additionalDifferentials: Bardet-Biedl syndrome type 11 (allelic, distinct multisystem phenotype)
additionalInvestigations: Next-generation sequencing gene panel or whole-exome sequencing including TRIM32
Muscle biopsy with histochemistry (dystrophic change, rimmed vacuoles or tubular aggregates)
Muscle MRI to characterise the pattern of involvement
Ophthalmological, renal and systemic review if ciliopathy overlap features are present
redFlags: Prominent cardiac symptoms suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
Retinal dystrophy, renal anomaly or polydactyly raising concern for Bardet-Biedl overlap
Rapidly progressive weakness inconsistent with the usually mild course
reference.prognosis: The course is generally mild and slowly progressive, with independent ambulation usually preserved for many years. Life expectancy is typically normal in the absence of unusual complications.
pitfalls: The mild, non-specific weakness is easily dismissed and the diagnosis missed.
Histological overlap with sarcotubular myopathy can cause classification confusion.
Assuming TRIM32 always causes myopathy overlooks the allelic Bardet-Biedl phenotype.
A normal or only mildly raised creatine kinase may falsely reassure the clinician.
references: Consensus classification of the limb-girdle muscular dystrophies
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy exists; management is conservative and supportive given the generally mild, slowly progressive course
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain proximal strength, function and mobility, with aids provided as required
Baseline and periodic respiratory function monitoring, though facial and respiratory involvement are usually mild or absent
Baseline and periodic cardiac assessment with ECG and echocardiography
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular follow-up to track slow progression
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, including testing for the recurrent p.Asp487Asn founder variant in Hutterite kindreds
